sections.title: Cloud versus on-premises benefits
points: Cloud computing delivers compute, storage, networking and more over the internet, on demand, with pay-as-you-use pricing.
CapEx (up-front hardware and datacenter spend) shifts to OpEx (ongoing, pay-for-what-you-use spend).
Resources are provisioned rapidly and capacity scales up or down with demand; adding cloud capacity costs less than expanding a datacenter.
The provider uses virtualization to serve many customers from shared hardware; you do not need to own physical servers.
Drawbacks to know: cloud offers fewer custom configuration options than on-premises, and it does not reduce administrative complexity by itself.

sections.title: Public cloud and hybrid cloud advantage
points: Public cloud: owned and operated by a provider; hardware is shared by multiple organizations (tenants), each isolated from the others.
Public cloud is not owned by the public, is not open to every member of the public, and is not crowd-sourced.
Hybrid cloud: on-premises resources plus public cloud capacity; extends existing resources without buying a whole new datacenter.

sections.title: Cloud Adoption Framework stages
points: The Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure guides adoption in stages: Strategy, Plan, Ready, Adopt, then Govern and Manage.
Define strategy (business justification and outcomes) comes first; planning, readying the environment, and adopting follow.

sections.title: Who is always responsible for what
points: Provider always: physical datacenter, hosts and network.
Customer always: information and data, devices/endpoints, and accounts and identities.
Identity and directory infrastructure is shared in IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
Customer responsibility is highest in IaaS, lower in PaaS, and lowest in SaaS.

sections.title: Responsibilities by service model
points: IaaS: customer manages OS, patching, applications and network controls; provider manages hardware and datacenter.
PaaS: provider manages OS and runtime; customer manages their application code and configuration, and user access; network controls are shared.
SaaS: provider runs the app, OS and infrastructure; customer configures the service, supplies data and manages access/identity.
Managed services such as Azure Backup are provider-operated platform services; you configure and use them.

sections.title: What moving to Azure VMs removes
points: Moving servers to Azure VMs (IaaS) eliminates hardware replacement and physical server security: the provider owns them.
Still yours on a VM: OS updates, application data backup and permissions to shared documents.

sections.title: Public cloud characteristics
points: Public cloud: all hardware is owned by the provider and shared between multiple tenants.
Characteristics: metered (pay-per-use) pricing, self-service management, no CapEx for hardware; not dedicated hardware.
An organization fully on the public cloud no longer needs its own datacenter; a private cloud or hybrid cloud still does.
Public cloud resources are virtual; you cannot add your own physical servers to it.

sections.title: Private cloud characteristics
points: Private cloud: resources used by one organization, often in its own datacenter; it gives complete control over resources and security.
A private cloud does not have to be disconnected from the internet.
Physical servers can be deployed in a private cloud or the on-premises part of a hybrid cloud, not in the public cloud.
Scaling a VM in the public cloud adds no capital expenditure for the customer; the provider carries it.

sections.title: Hybrid cloud
points: Hybrid cloud: combines on-premises (or private) resources with public cloud and lets workloads run in either place.
It requires an internal/on-premises network and a public cloud part; you can reach it by starting with public cloud, not only from a private cloud.
Typical examples: on-premises and Azure VMs connected together; an Azure web app querying an on-premises SQL Server.
It can extend internal capacity using public cloud resources.

sections.title: Choosing a cloud model by advantage
points: Public: no capital expenditure; pay for what you use.
Private: complete control over security and resources.
Hybrid: choice of on-premises or cloud-based resources.

sections.title: Matching workloads to cloud models
points: Public cloud: variable or growing demand, no hardware investment, fast provisioning.
Private cloud: need full control over hardware and security, or must keep resources on-premises.
Hybrid cloud: mix of both; keep some workloads on-premises and use the public cloud for extra capacity or specific services.

sections.title: Expenditure models
points: CapEx: up-front spending on physical infrastructure. OpEx: ongoing spending on services, paid as used.
Azure pay-as-you-go and other consumption-based cloud services are OpEx.
Elastic and scalable describe capabilities, not expenditure models.

sections.title: Consumption-based pricing
points: Consumption-based: you pay only for the resources you use, and can start or stop at any time; there is no fixed charge for unused capacity.
Pay-as-you-go is a consumption-based model; costs fall because you pay for extra capacity only when needed.
Serverless computing is an example of consumption-based pricing.

sections.title: CapEx versus OpEx examples
points: CapEx: building a datacenter, buying servers and other physical infrastructure.
OpEx: pay-as-you-go cloud usage, electricity, staff salaries, leasing or subscribing to software.
Migrating to Azure pay-as-you-go moves spending from CapEx to OpEx.

sections.title: Planning for Azure costs
points: Azure uses pay-as-you-go pricing.
A migrated website therefore brings recurring monthly usage costs, not an up-front purchase.

sections.title: Azure Functions
points: Azure Functions: serverless compute that runs your code in response to events (triggers) without you managing servers.
Functions are stateless by default; Durable Functions add state.
Not serverless: virtual machines, storage accounts and dedicated hosts.

sections.title: Azure Logic Apps
points: Logic Apps: serverless workflows built from triggers and actions using connectors, with little or no code.
Fits rule-based automation such as sending email notifications when an event occurs.
Compare: Functions runs code you write; Logic Apps orchestrates a workflow.

sections.title: High availability and fault tolerance
points: High availability: a service stays accessible with minimal downtime when a component fails; built into many platform services such as Azure SQL Data Warehouse.
Availability zones: separate datacenters in a region; spread VMs across zones to survive a datacenter failure.
Availability sets protect against rack and host failures, within one datacenter.

sections.title: Vertical versus horizontal scaling
points: Vertical scaling (scale up): add CPU or memory to an existing VM.
Horizontal scaling (scale out): add more instances, such as extra VMs; it can happen automatically or manually.
A service that supports more instances (20 versus 5) is more scalable.
Scaling to match demand also helps control costs.

sections.title: Elasticity and autoscaling
points: Elasticity: resources are allocated and released automatically as demand changes.
Autoscaling, such as VM scale sets, is elasticity.
Elasticity suits uneven usage (a heavy final week each month): you pay only for the capacity you use.

sections.title: Matching cloud benefits to needs
points: High availability: continuous user experience if a resource fails. Fault tolerance: stays available after a component fails.
Disaster recovery: restore a service after an outage (backup, replication).
Scalability/dynamic scalability: increase capacity as demand grows. Elasticity: do so dynamically.
Agility: quickly deploy, configure and adapt resources. Geo-distribution: deploy to regions close to users. Low latency: fast access.
Predictability covers performance and cost; manageability covers management of and in the cloud.

sections.title: Azure Machine Learning
points: Azure Machine Learning is the Azure service to build, train, test and deploy machine learning models.
It is the service to use for predictive analytics and AI solutions.

sections.title: Reliability and fault tolerance
points: Reliability: the system recovers from failures and keeps working.
Fault tolerance: a service stays available through a failure, including loss of a datacenter, by using redundant components across datacenters.
Elasticity, scalability and low latency address demand and speed, not failure.

sections.title: Predictability
points: Predictability covers performance: consistent behavior under load.
Predictability also covers cost: you can forecast and calculate what a service will cost.

sections.title: Azure Site Recovery
points: Azure Site Recovery provides disaster recovery for virtual machines by replicating them to a secondary region.
Disaster recovery restores a service after an outage; high availability keeps it running.

sections.title: Security and governance in the cloud
points: Cloud services can meet security, governance and compliance needs with built-in tools and templates.
Governance includes setting standards and auditing resources for compliance.
Security is shared: the provider secures the infrastructure; you secure your data and access.

sections.title: Manageability in the cloud
points: Management of the cloud: autoscaling, templates, monitoring and alerts to run resources.
Management in the cloud: portal, CLI, PowerShell and APIs to manage resources.

sections.title: Reducing administrative effort
points: Azure Reserved VM Instances are a pricing discount for a 1- or 3-year commitment; they do not reduce administration.
To cut the effort of deploying many VMs, use automation, templates or scale sets.

sections.title: IaaS characteristics
points: IaaS: you rent virtual infrastructure: VMs, storage and networks. Azure virtual machines are the standard example.
You install and manage the operating system, so IaaS fits lift-and-shift migrations.
PaaS and SaaS do not let you install an OS.

sections.title: When to choose IaaS
points: Choose IaaS for apps with prerequisite software, legacy databases or custom OS configuration.
You need full control of the server; the provider only manages hardware.

sections.title: PaaS characteristics
points: PaaS: a managed platform where you deploy code and the provider manages OS and infrastructure; no control of the host OS.
Azure App Service can scale automatically (autoscale), and memory/CPU is increased by changing the pricing tier.
You maintain application code; PaaS minimizes administrative effort for web apps.

sections.title: Identifying PaaS resources
points: PaaS examples: Azure App Service, Azure SQL Database, Azure Cosmos DB.
A SQL Server you install on a VM is IaaS; Azure SQL Database is managed by Azure.
A PaaS-only plan cannot include VMs; Storage accounts are not counted as PaaS here.

sections.title: SaaS characteristics
points: SaaS: provider-hosted, ready-to-use software; customer responsibility is smallest.
Microsoft 365 is SaaS; IaaS and PaaS require more management.

sections.title: Classifying Azure services
points: IaaS: Azure virtual machines, a DNS server on a VM, SQL Server on a VM.
PaaS: Azure App Service, Azure Functions, Azure SQL Database, Azure Cosmos DB, Azure Files.
SaaS: Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, Microsoft Intune.

sections.title: Picking the model for a requirement
points: IaaS: most control; hosts VMs; suits cloud file servers.
PaaS: custom apps with minimal OS effort; databases without OS maintenance.
SaaS: ready-made apps such as an accounting system.
Deploying virtual machines is IaaS, not PaaS or SaaS.
Need to change code but not manage the OS: PaaS. Need to work with the server OS: IaaS.

sections.title: Regions and datacenters
points: A region is a set of datacenters deployed within a latency-defined perimeter and connected by a dedicated low-latency regional network.
A geography (such as North America) contains multiple regions, so it is not a single region.
Not every region is guaranteed to have multiple datacenters; zones group one or more datacenters.
Many resources require you to choose a region at deploy time; data transfer between regions is billed, not always free.

sections.title: Azure Government
points: Azure Government is a separate Azure cloud built for US government compliance and security requirements.
Eligible customers: US federal, state, local and tribal government entities, and US contractors/partners that serve them.
Non-US government entities and contractors (for example European or Canadian) are not eligible.
Azure Government is operated by Microsoft.

sections.title: Azure China
points: Azure in China is a distinct, separate instance of Azure, physically isolated from global Azure.
It is operated by 21Vianet, not by Microsoft.
It does not have feature parity with global Azure and is not limited to access from inside China.

sections.title: What availability zones are
points: Availability zones are physically separate groups of one or more datacenters within a single Azure region, each with independent power, cooling and networking.
They are not spread across regions or continents, and they do not replicate data to multiple regions.
Not every Azure region supports availability zones; supporting regions have at least three.
Zones work with many services and with both Windows and Linux VMs, not only Windows Server VMs.

sections.title: Failures that zones protect against
points: Availability zones protect against datacenter-level (zone) failures, including smaller failures such as a rack or server.
They do not protect against a full region outage; use multiple regions for that.
Zone-redundant resources, including managed disks, survive the loss of one zone.
Failure scope, smallest to largest: server, datacenter/zone, region.

sections.title: Surviving a single datacenter failure
points: Deploying VMs to two or more availability zones keeps services running if one datacenter fails.
Deploying VMs to two or more regions also survives a datacenter failure (and a region failure), at greater cost and complexity.
Resource groups are only a management container and give no physical separation.
A single scale set is not by itself zone-resilient unless it is configured to span zones.

sections.title: VM SLA of 99.99 percent
points: Two or more VM instances spread across two or more availability zones in the same region give a 99.99 percent VM SLA.
Minimum for that SLA: 2 virtual machines in 2 availability zones.
An availability set (same datacenter) gives a lower SLA than zones.

sections.title: Datacenters, zones, and regions
points: A datacenter is the physical facility; Azure groups datacenters into availability zones and regions.
A region holds datacenters within a latency-defined perimeter, joined by a low-latency network.
An availability zone is a logical grouping of one or more physically separate datacenters with independent power, cooling and networking.

sections.title: Resource group behavior
points: A resource group stores metadata about its resources; its resources can be in different regions.
Each resource exists in exactly one resource group, and resource groups cannot be nested.
Deleting a resource group deletes all resources in it.
Resources can communicate with resources in other resource groups.
Tags and permissions: permissions assigned on a group are inherited by its resources; tags are not inherited automatically.

sections.title: Where resources are placed
points: Every Azure resource, such as a VM, is deployed into a resource group within a subscription.
A storage account is a resource itself, not a container for VMs.

sections.title: Subscriptions, tenants, and administrators
points: A subscription trusts exactly one Microsoft Entra tenant; a tenant can have many subscriptions.
You can change the directory associated with a subscription.
If a subscription expires, the Entra tenant is not deleted.
Subscriptions are managed with Entra accounts, not only Microsoft accounts; a subscription has one account administrator.
Separate Entra directories per division create more admin overhead than subscriptions.

sections.title: Multiple subscriptions and moving resources
points: One account can manage multiple subscriptions, and a company can use resources from many.
Subscriptions cannot be merged; instead move resources between subscriptions.
VMs and their associated resources can be moved to a different subscription.

sections.title: Subscription as billing and limit boundary
points: Create a subscription first as the container for billing and resources when starting in Azure.
Costs are billed per subscription, so give each department its own subscription to use different payment options.
Subscription quotas/limits are raised by creating a new support request (quota increase).

sections.title: Free trial and ownership
points: After a free trial expires you cannot start VMs; convert to pay-as-you-go to continue.
The Owner role manages resources but does not transfer the subscription; billing account administrators do.
A spending limit on a trial is fixed.

sections.title: Management groups
points: Management groups sit above subscriptions and let you apply governance, such as Azure Policy and access control, across multiple subscriptions.
Resource groups organize resources inside one subscription and cannot span subscriptions.
Azure Policy defines rules; management groups define the scope where they apply.

sections.title: Scope hierarchy
points: Order, top to bottom: management group, subscription, resource group, resource (such as a VM).
Settings such as policy and access assigned at a higher scope are inherited below.

sections.title: Segmenting Azure by department
points: Use separate subscriptions and/or resource groups to segment resources for departments, each with its own administrator.
Multiple regions do not provide administrative segmentation.
Multiple Entra directories add administrative effort and are not the usual approach.

sections.title: Compare compute services
points: Virtual machines: IaaS; full OS control and OS-level virtualization.
Container Instances: run containers without managing VMs; portable app environment.
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) and Container Instances both manage containers.
App Service: PaaS to build, deploy and scale web apps.
Functions: serverless, event-triggered code. VM Scale Sets: groups of identical VMs.

sections.title: IoT services
points: IoT Hub: managed service for bidirectional communication between IoT devices and Azure; ingests data from millions of sensors.
IoT Central: fully managed SaaS to connect, monitor and manage IoT devices at scale.
Azure Sphere: secured MCU hardware, custom Linux OS and security service for IoT devices.
Data Lake Storage holds large volumes of ingested data.

sections.title: AI, analytics, and app services
points: Azure Machine Learning: build, test and deploy predictive analytics.
Azure Bot Service: conversational bots. Functions: serverless code.
Databricks: Apache Spark-based analytics. Application Insights: detects anomalies in web apps.
Cosmos DB is a database, not a predictive analytics tool.

sections.title: Azure DevTest Labs
points: DevTest Labs reduces administrative effort for creating and removing many Windows or Linux VMs repeatedly, with templates and policies.
It is not a compute type like VMs or scale sets; it is a lab-management service for dev/test VMs.

sections.title: Azure Virtual Desktop
points: Azure Virtual Desktop is a desktop and app virtualization service delivering cloud-hosted Windows from any location.
It supports both full desktops and published apps.
Session hosts are not limited to Windows 10; Windows 11 and Windows Server are also supported.
A host pool supports multi-session, so connections can exceed the number of session hosts.

sections.title: Scale sets and availability sets
points: VM Scale Sets: identically configured VMs that can scale in and out automatically.
Availability sets: group VMs into fault domains and update domains within a datacenter.
Availability zones are separate datacenters; load balancers distribute traffic.

sections.title: Azure Spot virtual machines
points: Spot VMs use unused Azure compute capacity at deep discounts; capacity can be reclaimed.
Reserved VM Instances are a committed-term discount, not unused-capacity pricing.

sections.title: Deploying many temporary VMs
points: Azure DevTest Labs minimizes effort to create and remove many VMs.
Microsoft Managed Desktop manages end-user desktops; it is not for deploying batches of VMs.
Scale sets scale identical VMs, not customized Windows and Linux mixes.

sections.title: VM dependencies
points: Every Azure VM needs a virtual network (its network interface connects to a subnet), plus a disk and compute.
A public IP address, service endpoint or Azure Firewall is optional.

sections.title: Content delivery network
points: A CDN caches content such as video at edge locations near users for best worldwide playback.
Application Gateway, ExpressRoute and Traffic Manager do not cache content at the edge.

sections.title: App Service plan tiers
points: Free and Shared run on shared VMs and cannot scale out.
Basic, Standard and Premium run on dedicated VMs; features such as custom domains, TLS/SSL, autoscale and slots depend on tier.
Needs such as multiple dedicated instances with load balancing, custom domain and SSL point to Standard over Free, Shared or Basic.
Costs: choose the lowest tier that meets all requirements.

sections.title: Virtual network basics
points: A virtual network provides isolation and segmentation; use separate VNets for separate network segments.
VNets in the same region are not connected by default; VNet names are unique within a resource group.
Address spaces can overlap in a subscription but must not overlap for peered VNets.
Peering can connect any two VNets, across regions or subscriptions.

sections.title: Network security groups
points: An NSG filters inbound and outbound traffic with allow/deny rules; it controls ports and connection types between VMs.
Associate an NSG with a subnet or a network interface, not with a virtual network.
Sources can be IP addresses/CIDR, service tags or application security groups.
Default rules allow VNet and outbound internet traffic and deny other inbound traffic, so NSGs do not block all traffic.
A local network gateway is not a traffic filter.

sections.title: Allowing internet access to a VM
points: Allow inbound HTTP/ports to a VM by modifying the NSG rules.
Traffic Manager is DNS-based load balancing and does not open ports.
DDoS protection does not allow ports either.

sections.title: Firewall and DDoS protection
points: Azure Firewall NAT (DNAT) rules let internet users reach a server in a virtual network; network and application rules filter traffic.
One Azure Firewall can centrally limit inbound traffic across virtual networks.
DDoS Protection defends against attacks and provides attack reports.

sections.title: Hybrid connectivity
points: Site-to-Site VPN: on-premises VPN device to an Azure VPN gateway over an encrypted tunnel on the internet.
Point-to-Site (P2S) VPN connects individual remote client computers to a VNet.
ExpressRoute: dedicated private connection that does not use the public internet; uses BGP, operates at layer 3; multiple circuits supported.

To connect on-premises to Azure VMs you need a virtual network (VNet) and a virtual network gateway. The gateway lives in a dedicated 'GatewaySubnet' inside that VNet; a local network gateway represents the on-premises VPN device.
When asked for the two resources, the answer pair is the virtual network gateway and the virtual network.

sections.title: Azure DNS
points: Azure DNS hosts custom DNS domains and supports both public and private zones.
Azure VMs can register names in Azure DNS automatically.

sections.title: User-defined routes and appliances
points: A network virtual appliance is a VM that performs a network function such as a firewall.
User-defined routes can control traffic beyond a single VNet's subnets.
NSGs can contain multiple inbound and outbound rules.

sections.title: Tools for running Azure scripts
points: PowerShell scripts run from Windows, Linux or macOS with Azure PowerShell installed.
Azure CLI works on Linux/macOS/Windows; Cloud Shell runs in a browser from any OS.

sections.title: Keeping storage traffic off the internet
points: A service endpoint keeps traffic from a virtual network to an Azure service (such as Storage) on the Microsoft backbone network.
A private endpoint gives the service a private IP address in your VNet.
A public endpoint is reachable over the internet; NSGs and VPN Gateway do not make PaaS traffic private.

sections.title: Azure Storage services
points: Blob: very large unstructured objects like video. Files: network file shares (SMB) mapped as drives.
Queue: reliable messaging between applications. Table: key/attribute NoSQL store.
Disk storage: VM disks; unmanaged VM disks are stored in blob containers.
Only Blob supports the Archive access tier.

sections.title: Database and analytics services
points: Cosmos DB: globally distributed NoSQL, JSON documents, multi-region writes.
SQL Database: managed relational database. Synapse Analytics: MPP data warehouse.
HDInsight: managed Hadoop/Spark clusters. Data Lake: store large analytics data.
Machine Learning predicts; IoT Hub ingests device data; Functions runs serverless code.

sections.title: Tier minimum retention and cost
points: Hot: frequently accessed, highest storage cost, lowest access cost.
Cool: infrequent, at least 30 days. Cold: at least 90 days. Archive: at least 180 days, lowest storage cost.
Deleting or moving data before the minimum period triggers an early deletion fee.

sections.title: Archive rehydration
points: Archive is offline: blobs can't be read until rehydrated to hot, cool or cold; this can take hours.
Archive can't be the default account tier.
Archive is supported only for LRS, GRS and RA-GRS accounts.

sections.title: Setting access tiers
points: The account default tier is hot or cool (or cold), and blob tiers can be changed after upload.
Archive is set per blob, not at account level.
Cool and archive are not recommended for active data; archive suits long-term backups.
Tiering applies to block blobs, not premium storage.

sections.title: Number of copies
points: LRS keeps 3 copies in one datacenter.
ZRS 3 copies across zones; GRS 6 copies (3 + 3 in secondary region); GZRS 6 copies.
Storage always keeps at least three copies, but LRS isn't backed up to another datacenter.

sections.title: Read access to the secondary region
points: GRS does not allow reads from the secondary; RA-GRS does.
Choose RA-GRS or RA-GZRS for data on multiple nodes in separate regions with reads from both.

sections.title: Ordering redundancy options
points: Least to most redundant: LRS, ZRS, GRS (GZRS highest).
LRS protects drive/rack failures; ZRS adds zone failures; GRS adds region failures.

sections.title: Premium block blob redundancy
points: Premium block blob accounts support LRS and ZRS only, not geo-redundancy.
GRS, GZRS and their read-access variants are available for standard general-purpose v2 accounts.

sections.title: Premium account types
points: Premium performance accounts include block blobs and file shares (and page blobs).
Standard general-purpose v2 is the standard account type, not a premium type.
Premium accounts use SSD storage for low latency.

sections.title: Creating storage accounts
points: Create an Azure file share inside a storage account.
Storage account names must be globally unique across Azure, regardless of region or subscription.

sections.title: File transfer and sync tools
points: AzCopy: command-line utility to copy blobs or files to or from a storage account.
Azure Storage Explorer: graphical app for managing storage, not a migration service.
Azure File Sync: syncs Windows Server files with an Azure Files file share.

sections.title: Data Box and Azure Migrate
points: Azure Data Box is a physical device to move large amounts of data quickly and inexpensively.
Azure Migrate discovers, assesses and migrates on-premises servers and workloads.
Azure File Sync syncs files and Databricks is an analytics service.

sections.title: Entra ID as the cloud identity provider
points: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is a cloud-based identity and access management service. It needs no domain controllers on Azure virtual machines.
It is the built-in authentication and authorization service for Azure, Microsoft 365 and other SaaS apps; applications request security tokens from it.
Create and manage users in Microsoft Entra ID (Azure portal > Microsoft Entra ID > Users), not in Subscriptions, Resource groups or Virtual machines.
A user can hold several licenses, for example Microsoft 365 plus other Microsoft cloud services. Licensing is not limited to one per user.
Identities from third-party providers or on-premises AD can be trusted through federation, so access to Azure is not limited to cloud-only accounts.

sections.title: Syncing on-premises AD to Entra ID
points: Microsoft Entra Connect (Entra Connect Sync) synchronizes identities from on-premises Active Directory to Microsoft Entra ID.
To keep users working after moving resources to Azure and retiring the datacenter, sync the existing AD accounts (and optionally password hashes) to Entra ID.
Synced users keep their existing credentials, so impact on users is minimal. No re-creation or password reset is needed.
MFA adds sign-in security but does not create identities in the cloud. Guest accounts are for external users, not for migrating your own staff.

sections.title: Devices, groups and SSO in Entra ID
points: Windows 10/11 devices can be Microsoft Entra joined (or hybrid joined) so users sign in with Entra credentials; iOS and Android devices can be registered.
Group Policy is an on-premises Active Directory feature; you cannot create Group Policy objects in Microsoft Entra ID (device management uses Intune).
Groups in Entra ID support dynamic membership rules that add or remove members automatically from user or device attributes.
Users are organized with groups and administrative units. Resource groups organize Azure resources, not users.
Entra ID provides single sign-on (SSO) and can manage access to on-premises apps (for example through Application Proxy).

sections.title: Analyzing Entra security events with Sentinel
points: Microsoft Sentinel is a cloud-native SIEM/SOAR that collects and analyzes security events, including Entra ID sign-in and audit logs, through data connectors.
Microsoft Entra Connect only synchronizes identities. Key Vault stores secrets. Synapse Analytics is an analytics service, not a security-event service.

sections.title: Authentication versus authorization
points: Authentication proves identity: verifying credentials of a user or service. Authorization decides what an authenticated identity is allowed to access.
Federation, synchronization and ticketing are different concepts; Conditional Access evaluates sign-in signals to allow or deny access.
SSO lets users sign in once with one set of credentials for several apps. It does not require the Microsoft Authenticator app.
MFA requires more than one verification element (for example password plus a phone prompt) to identify a user.

sections.title: Single sign-on with Entra ID
points: Microsoft Entra ID enables SSO to many cloud and on-premises applications with a single set of credentials.
Key Vault stores secrets, application security groups group VMs for network rules, and Defender for Cloud assesses security posture. None provide SSO.

sections.title: How multi-factor authentication works
points: MFA combines factors from categories: something you know (password), something you have (phone, security key), something you are (biometric).
Valid verification methods include Microsoft Authenticator, SMS, voice call and hardware tokens. Photo ID and passport numbers are not methods.
MFA works in cloud-only environments. It does not require syncing on-premises identities or deploying federation.
MFA can be required for administrators only or for any user account.

sections.title: Password, MFA and passwordless compared
points: Password only: low security, convenient. It is the weakest option.
MFA: high security but adds steps, so less convenient.
Passwordless (Windows Hello for Business, Microsoft Authenticator, FIDO2 security keys): high security and convenient, with no password to steal.

sections.title: Microsoft Entra External ID basics
points: External identities let people outside your organization (partners, vendors, customers) access your apps and resources using their own identities.
B2B collaboration: invite external users as guests who sign in with their own organizational or social identity.
B2C / customer identity: provide sign-up and sign-in for consumer-facing apps, separate from the workforce directory.

sections.title: Conditional Access evaluates sign-in signals
points: Conditional Access is the Microsoft Entra policy engine that combines signals (user, location, device, application, risk) to make access decisions.
Decisions include block access, grant access, or grant with requirements such as MFA or a compliant device.
To limit access to apps to users whose devices meet requirements (such as being compliant or patched), create a Conditional Access policy.
Azure Firewall, Bastion and Azure Policy do not make sign-in decisions for Entra-integrated applications; managed identities and Intune are not signal engines.

sections.title: Identity Protection, PIM and Defender for Identity
points: Microsoft Entra ID Protection detects risky sign-ins and users (such as anonymous IP addresses) and drives risk-based policies: require MFA or force a password change.
Privileged Identity Management (PIM) manages just-in-time, time-bound and approved elevation of privileged roles. It does not react to risky sign-ins.
Microsoft Defender for Identity (formerly Azure ATP) uses sensors installed on on-premises domain controllers to detect threats and compromised identities.
Microsoft Entra Connect Health monitors the health of the sync infrastructure, not sign-in risk.

sections.title: Scope and assigning Azure roles
points: Azure RBAC scopes: management group, subscription, resource group, resource. Assignments at a parent scope are inherited by child scopes.
To give a user permissions on many VMs at once, place them in the same resource group and assign the role at the resource group.
Assign roles from Access control (IAM) on the chosen scope (management group, subscription, resource group or resource).
Azure RBAC roles also grant permissions to services such as Azure Virtual Desktop. Tags, resource groups and application security groups do not grant permissions.

sections.title: Roles and role assignments
points: Azure has built-in roles (Owner, Contributor, Reader) and supports custom roles when built-in ones don't fit.
A user can have multiple role assignments, and a scope such as a resource group can have the Owner role assigned to multiple users.

sections.title: Identity sources and federation
points: Access to Azure resources is not limited to Entra ID accounts: federation allows identities from on-premises AD or other providers to be used.
Azure has built-in authentication (Entra ID) and authorization (RBAC) services.

sections.title: Network isolation is not RBAC
points: Azure routes traffic automatically between subnets in a virtual network, so all VMs in one virtual network can communicate by default.
To prevent a VM from connecting to others, deploy it to a separate virtual network (or restrict traffic with NSGs).
Resource group, OS and number of NICs do not isolate network traffic; resource groups are logical containers for management.

sections.title: Zero Trust principles
points: Zero Trust assumes no implicit trust based on network location. Every access request is authenticated, authorized and encrypted.
Verify explicitly: use all available signals such as identity, location, device health and data classification.
Use least privilege access: limit access with just-in-time and just-enough access and risk-based adaptive policies.
Assume breach: minimize blast radius with segmentation, end-to-end encryption, and use analytics to detect threats.

sections.title: Defense-in-depth layers
points: Layers from outside in: physical security, identity and access, perimeter, network, compute, application, data.
Physical security: surveillance cameras and datacenter access controls. Identity and access: MFA, conditional access, SSO.
Perimeter: DDoS protection and firewalls at the network edge. Network: segmentation and NSGs. Compute: patching and endpoint protection.
Application: secure code and secrets management. Data: encryption of stored and transmitted data.

sections.title: Azure Key Vault for secrets and certificates
points: Azure Key Vault securely stores and controls access to secrets, keys, and certificates (passwords, API keys, connection strings, TLS certificates).
Use it to avoid exposing administrative credentials in automated deployment scripts; applications and servers retrieve secrets at runtime.
Azure Information Protection classifies and protects documents and email; MFA verifies identity; Defender for Cloud assesses posture. None store certificates or secrets.
Storage accounts are not designed for secure secret management.

sections.title: Azure Disk Encryption prerequisite
points: Azure Disk Encryption uses BitLocker (Windows) or DM-Crypt (Linux) and stores encryption keys and secrets in Azure Key Vault.
Create the Key Vault before enabling disk encryption on the VM.

sections.title: Network filtering versus encryption
points: Azure Firewall and network security groups filter traffic by rules. They do not encrypt traffic.
Encryption in transit comes from protocols such as TLS/HTTPS or IPsec VPN, which VMs can use.
To make a VM reachable over HTTP, allow inbound port 80 (for example with an NSG rule). A DDoS protection plan only mitigates attacks, it does not open access.

sections.title: Defender for Cloud posture and compliance
points: Microsoft Defender for Cloud (formerly Security Center and Azure Defender) is a cloud security posture management (CSPM) and workload protection (CWP) platform.
It shows secure score, security recommendations, and a regulatory compliance dashboard with downloadable reports.
It monitors Azure resources and also on-premises and multicloud resources.
Basic features such as continuous assessment, recommendations and secure score are free; enhanced security features (Defender plans) are paid.

sections.title: Just-in-time VM access
points: Just-in-time (JIT) VM access, a Defender for Cloud feature, locks down inbound management ports (such as RDP and SSH) on VMs.
Access is opened temporarily on request for a limited time, reducing attack surface.
Bastion provides browser-based RDP/SSH, Firewall filters traffic, Front Door is a web delivery service. They are not the JIT feature.

sections.title: Microsoft Sentinel as SIEM
points: Microsoft Sentinel is a cloud-native SIEM (security information and event management) and SOAR (security orchestration, automation and response) solution.
Data connectors collect logs from Azure, Microsoft 365, Entra ID, Windows firewall logs on VMs and more. Data is stored in a Log Analytics workspace, not a storage account.
It analyzes events with analytics rules, creates incidents, and can remediate automatically using automation rules and playbooks.
Azure Analysis Services, Cognitive Services and Information Protection are not SIEM solutions.

sections.title: Automating response with Sentinel playbooks
points: Playbooks are Azure Logic Apps workflows that run in response to alerts or incidents to automate and orchestrate threat response.
They are attached to analytics rules or automation rules and can run automatically.
Workbooks visualize collected data; they do not respond to threats. Adaptive network hardening and adaptive application controls belong to Defender for Cloud.

sections.title: Matching security services to tasks
points: Microsoft Sentinel: SIEM, analyze security logs. Microsoft Defender for Cloud: secure score, recommendations, compliance. Azure Key Vault: store secrets, keys and certificates.
Microsoft Entra ID: identity and sign-in. Azure Lighthouse: cross-tenant management for service providers.

sections.title: Azure Firewall scope
points: Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful firewall as a service with central policies and logging across multiple subscriptions and virtual networks.
NSGs and application security groups filter at the subnet/NIC level within one virtual network scope. DDoS Protection mitigates volumetric attacks.

sections.title: What influences the cost of a resource
points: Cost factors: resource type and size, service tier, Azure region, and usage. Prices differ between regions for the same service.
Outbound data volume affects cost; the type of processed data does not. Inbound transfer does not add cost.
Storage: the price varies by region, and read/write operations and cross-region transfers are billable in general-purpose v2 accounts.
A reservation commits to a resource for a term for a discount; it does not reserve capacity at a specific datacenter.
An Azure SQL Database cannot be stopped to save money; scale the tier or use serverless auto-pause.

sections.title: Bandwidth: inbound versus outbound
points: Inbound data transfer (ingress) to Azure is free, including over VPN and ExpressRoute.
Outbound data transfer (egress) from Azure to on-premises or the internet is billed and its price varies by region.
Data transfer between services in the same region is not charged; transfers between regions are billed for the source's outbound traffic.
Resource groups are logical containers and incur no cost.

sections.title: Virtual machine billing and cost flexibility
points: Stopped (Deallocated) VMs aren't billed for compute, but disks (OS and data) and other resources like public IPs continue to incur charges.
A VM stopped from inside the guest OS stays allocated and is still billed. Stop (deallocate) it from the portal to stop compute charges.
Two VMs of the same size do not always cost the same: disks, region, OS, licensing and usage time all differ.
Reservations and savings plans lower VM cost versus pay-as-you-go. The cloud shifts spending from CapEx to OpEx and allows a mix.

sections.title: Reservations and Azure Hybrid Benefit
points: Azure Reservations are available for one-year or three-year terms. Three years is the longest term for reserved VM instances and gives the highest discount.
Azure Hybrid Benefit lets you use existing Windows Server and SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance (or subscriptions) on Azure to reduce licensing cost.
Deallocating VMs or setting budgets doesn't reduce license cost. Budgets only alert; reservations discount compute rather than licenses.

sections.title: Azure free account limits
points: A free account gives $200 credit for the first 30 days plus limited quantities of certain services free for 12 months.
Only a subset of services and tiers are included. Credit or free quantities expire, after which pay-as-you-go rates apply.
Limits apply per service (for example 5 GB blob storage), so unlimited web apps or 2 TB uploads are not included.
Free accounts are limited per person and not repeatable on the same Microsoft account.

sections.title: Agreements and Marketplace pricing
points: An Enterprise Agreement (EA) requires a predetermined (commitment) spend. Outbound traffic cost differs by region.
Third-party Marketplace offerings are priced by the publisher, not by Microsoft.

sections.title: Idle resources that do and don't cost
points: Public IP addresses (standard SKU) are billed, so deleting unused ones reduces cost.
Network interfaces, Microsoft Entra users and groups, and resource groups are not billed. Deleting them does not reduce cost.

sections.title: TCO calculator
points: The Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculator compares the cost of running workloads on-premises with running them in Azure.
It includes datacenter costs such as hardware, electricity, space, and IT labor, so it can show savings from reduced power use after migrating.
It produces shareable reports with graphs and is available to anyone, with no Azure account required.

sections.title: Pricing calculator versus TCO
points: The Azure pricing calculator estimates the monthly cost of Azure services you configure (region, size, tier, usage), for new deployments.
Azure Migrate assesses servers for migration readiness and sizing; Database Migration Assistant checks SQL compatibility; neither estimates power savings.

sections.title: Cost analysis in Cost Management
points: Cost Management is available to anyone with access to a billing account, subscription, resource group or management group, including pay-as-you-go subscriptions.
Cost analysis views costs by scope (management group, subscription, resource group) and usage over time, such as the last three months.
No Enterprise Agreement or Software Assurance is required.

sections.title: Budgets and cost alerts
points: Budgets in Cost Management track spend against a threshold and send email alerts when actual or forecasted cost reaches a percentage.
Budgets only alert; they do not stop resources. Advisor recommendations and IAM do not send cost-limit alerts.
Tags help categorize costs but a budget is what tracks cost against a limit.

sections.title: Reducing cost of idle resources
points: Delete unused public IP addresses, which are billed. Unused user accounts, groups and network interfaces are not billed.
Azure Advisor cost recommendations identify idle resources.

sections.title: Stopping virtual machines to save cost
points: Stop a VM from the Azure portal (or CLI) so it is deallocated and compute billing stops.
Shutting down or disconnecting from inside the guest OS leaves the VM allocated and still billed.

sections.title: Tags for cost reporting and accountability
points: Tags are key-value metadata (for example Department = Finance) applied to resources, resource groups and subscriptions.
Cost reports can be grouped and filtered by tag, so you can report cost per department, office or cost center and track budgets.
Locks, policies and templates do not group costs; tags do. Budgets and alerts do not identify who owns a resource.

sections.title: Tag rules and limits
points: A resource can have multiple tags (up to 50 tag name-value pairs on most resources).
Resources do not inherit tags from the resource group or subscription; use Azure Policy to apply or inherit tags.
Tags can be applied through ARM templates. Tags are metadata and do not enforce naming standards; Azure Policy does that.

sections.title: Trust Center and Service Trust Portal
points: Microsoft Trust Center is a public site with information on security, privacy, compliance offerings, policies and features across Microsoft cloud products. No Azure subscription is needed.
Use it to check whether Azure complies with your regional or industry requirements. It is not part of Defender for Cloud.
The Service Trust Portal publishes audit reports, whitepapers and compliance resources for Microsoft cloud services.
Sign in with a Microsoft cloud services account to reach some content; My Library saves documents in one place.

sections.title: Compliance Manager
points: Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager assesses and tracks regulatory compliance for Microsoft cloud services with pre-built assessments, improvement actions and a compliance score.
It is opened from the Microsoft Purview portal (formerly Microsoft 365 compliance center) using an admin account.
Defender for Cloud also has a regulatory compliance dashboard for evaluating Azure resources against standards such as ISO 27001.
Cloud Shell, Azure Advisor, Service Health and Knowledge Center do not track regulatory standards.

sections.title: Microsoft privacy and data protection documents
points: Microsoft Privacy Statement: which personal data Microsoft collects, how it is processed, and for what purpose.
Online Services Terms (now the Product Terms and Data Protection Addendum): the contractual commitments for online services.
Data Protection Addendum: data processing and security terms, including processing, transfer, retention and deletion of customer data.

sections.title: Compliance standards and regulations
points: ISO: international standards body across all industries. NIST: US standards institute used by the US government.
GDPR: EU regulation on data privacy and protection; it applies to organizations that offer goods or services to people in the EU. Azure can be used to build GDPR-compliant solutions.
Azure Government: a dedicated public cloud for US federal, state and local government agencies.

sections.title: Information protection and data governance
points: Microsoft Purview Information Protection (formerly Azure Information Protection) classifies and protects documents and emails using sensitivity labels.
Labels can encrypt documents and email, and apply visual markings such as watermarks automatically when sensitive data like credit card numbers is detected.
It protects documents and emails, not network traffic, storage accounts or SQL databases.
Microsoft Purview provides data discovery and classification and data governance; it is not a backup service.

sections.title: Policy versus locks, tags and blueprints
points: Azure Policy enforces rules on resource properties, such as allowed regions or allowed VM sizes, and reports compliance.
Resource locks prevent deletion or modification; tags are metadata for organization and cost tracking; blueprints package templates, policies, role assignments for repeatable environments.
To restrict where or what resources can be created (and still allow others) use Policy. Locks and RBAC roles cannot target a resource type or region.
Management groups organize subscriptions; reservations are billing discounts.

sections.title: Policy definitions and initiatives
points: A policy definition is a single business rule that describes a compliance condition and the effect.
An initiative definition is a collection of policy definitions grouped toward one goal and assigned as a single item.

sections.title: Assigning policy and its effect
points: A policy or initiative is assigned to a scope: management group, subscription, resource group or resource.
The assignment applies to all resources within the scope; it blocks or audits non-compliant deployments depending on the effect.
Existing non-compliant resources are flagged non-compliant, not removed.

sections.title: Delete versus read-only locks
points: Two lock levels: CanNotDelete (Delete in the portal) and ReadOnly. Delete lock: authorized users can read and modify but not delete.
ReadOnly lock: users can only read, not update or delete; it is like the Reader role for everyone.
To prevent accidental deletion while allowing changes (such as creating containers), use a Delete lock; to block changes and deletes, use ReadOnly.
A ReadOnly lock still prevents deletion, but a Delete lock does not block modification.

sections.title: Lock scope and inheritance
points: Locks can be applied to subscriptions, resource groups and resources, not to users, administrative units or policies.
A lock at a parent scope is inherited by all child resources, including resources added later. The most restrictive lock wins.
A resource can have multiple locks. You can add a Delete lock to a resource that has a ReadOnly lock.
Any Azure resource can have a lock.

sections.title: Locks override user permissions
points: A lock applies to all users and roles, including owners and global administrators.
To delete a locked resource group, first remove the lock; no tag or policy change replaces that.

sections.title: Locks versus Azure Policy
points: A Policy assignment does not delete or modify existing resources. Non-compliant resources are flagged but continue to function.
Locks restrict operations on a resource; Policy governs which resources can be created and their configuration.

sections.title: Azure portal: web-based management
points: The Azure portal is a browser-based console at portal.azure.com for creating and managing all your Azure resources in one place.
Because it runs in a browser, it works on any OS and device: Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android. Nothing has to be installed.
It needs an internet connection and a sign-in. Command-line management is a separate option (Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, Cloud Shell).
From a phone or tablet, use the Azure portal or Cloud Shell; locally installed tools (Windows PowerShell, Azure Storage Explorer) are not the answer for mobile.
Cloud services and other resources can be managed from the portal, the command line, or APIs; management is not limited to Windows devices.

sections.title: Marketplace and portal blades
points: Azure Marketplace: catalog to find, try, and buy Microsoft and third-party solutions, such as VM images and security appliances, to deploy to a subscription.
Microsoft Store is for consumer/Microsoft products, not Azure deployments; a subscription is a billing and access boundary, not a store.
Monitor blade: monitor health and performance of services and resources.
Advisor blade: personalized recommendations, including security; Microsoft Defender for Cloud is the dedicated security posture service.

sections.title: Azure Cloud Shell
points: Cloud Shell is an authenticated, browser-accessible shell for managing Azure. Nothing needs to be installed locally.
Start it from a web browser: the Azure portal toolbar or shell.azure.com. It works from any OS, including Android tablets and Chrome OS.
You choose Bash or PowerShell as the experience. Azure CLI (az) commands run in both.
To create a VM from an Android tablet: the Azure portal, Cloud Shell (Bash), or Cloud Shell (PowerShell). The PowerApps portal does not manage Azure VMs.
Azure CLI is not installed by default on Windows 11; Cloud Shell has it preinstalled.

sections.title: Azure CLI: where it runs
points: Azure CLI (az commands) is cross-platform: install it on Windows, macOS, or Linux.
On Windows you can run az from Command Prompt or Windows PowerShell (or Windows Terminal). Tools like Firewall or Network and Sharing Center are unrelated.
Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell both run on Windows, Linux, and macOS; the Azure portal works in any browser.
So a Windows 10, Ubuntu, or macOS computer can use the Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, and the portal.

sections.title: Azure PowerShell: running PowerShell scripts
points: Azure PowerShell (the Az module) manages Azure with PowerShell cmdlets and is cross-platform: Windows, macOS, and Linux.
To run a PowerShell script that creates resources you need PowerShell with the Az module installed, or Cloud Shell (PowerShell) from a browser.
Having only Azure CLI tools installed does not let you run PowerShell scripts; CLI uses az commands.
The Az module needs a supported PowerShell version (Windows PowerShell 5.1 or PowerShell 7.x). Old PowerShell Core 6.0 is out of support.
Valid hosts: Windows with the Az module, Chrome OS using Cloud Shell, or macOS/Linux with a supported PowerShell and Az.

sections.title: Azure Arc projects non-Azure resources
points: Azure Arc extends Azure Resource Manager to resources outside Azure: you project them into Azure and manage them like Azure resources.
On-premises Windows Server and Linux servers (physical or virtual) can be managed from the Azure portal by connecting them to Arc.
Azure Arc is the answer for a unified way to project and manage non-Azure resources in ARM.
Not Arc: Azure AD Connect syncs identities; Azure Migrate assesses and moves workloads; Front Door is a web traffic service; AKS runs Kubernetes in Azure.

sections.title: Arc for hybrid and multicloud governance
points: Arc supports servers, Kubernetes clusters, and data services (SQL Server, PostgreSQL) hosted on-premises, at the edge, or in other clouds.
It applies Azure management and governance (Azure Policy, Azure Monitor, RBAC) consistently across hybrid and multicloud environments.
Arc-enabled Kubernetes can manage clusters at scale, and third-party or non-Azure databases can be managed as Arc-enabled data services.
Azure Policy defines rules; Arc is what extends compliance and monitoring reach to resources outside Azure.

sections.title: Azure DevTest Labs
points: DevTest Labs lets teams quickly create and remove environments (VMs) from ARM templates, with policies, quotas, and auto-shutdown to control cost.
It minimizes admin effort for developers who repeatedly deploy and delete many VMs.
Scale sets: autoscale identical VMs. Reserved VM Instances: discounted committed-use pricing. Azure Virtual Desktop: hosted desktops.

sections.title: Azure DevOps services: Repos
points: Azure DevOps is a set of development services: Repos, Pipelines, Boards, Test Plans, and Artifacts.
Azure Repos: Git (and TFVC) version control tools to manage code.
Azure Pipelines: CI/CD builds and deployments. Azure Boards: work tracking.
Infrastructure as code (templates, scripts) is stored and versioned in source control such as Repos.

sections.title: ARM templates: repeatable deployments
points: ARM templates are declarative JSON files that define infrastructure; this is infrastructure as code.
One template can define many resources and be deployed repeatedly with the same result, so each resource does not need its own template.
Deploy templates through the Azure portal, Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, or REST API.
For identical resources across business units, use ARM templates. Management groups organize subscriptions; API Management publishes APIs; scale sets scale VMs.
Resource groups are logical containers; Azure Policy enforces rules on what can be deployed. Neither deploys resources from a definition.

sections.title: ARM as the management layer and APIs
points: Azure Resource Manager is the deployment and management service for Azure. Every tool (portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs) calls the ARM REST APIs.
A desktop application interacts with Azure and manages resources by calling APIs (REST/SDKs).
Templates describe what to deploy; CLI and Cloud Shell are tools that call the APIs.

sections.title: What Azure Advisor does
points: Advisor is a free personalized cloud consultant: it analyzes your resource configuration and usage and recommends best practices.
Recommendation categories: Reliability, Security, Operational excellence, Performance, and Cost.
It covers resources across multiple subscriptions and can alert you to new recommendations.
It does not estimate costs of a planned solution (pricing calculator), assess on-premises migration (Azure Migrate), or integrate AD (Azure AD Connect).
Advisor does not list backed-up VMs, configure VM network settings, or set a deadline for acting; acting on security advice improves your secure score.

sections.title: Advisor cost recommendations
points: Advisor identifies underutilized or idle resources, such as VMs with low CPU use, and suggests resizing, shutting down, or buying reservations.
Use Advisor to get recommendations that reduce Azure costs.
Cost Management + Billing analyzes spending and budgets. The pricing calculator estimates new deployments. Reservations are a discount, not an analyzer.
Service Health reports Azure incidents, not savings.

sections.title: Advisor versus related services
points: Azure Advisor: recommendations to improve an environment. Azure Monitor: health and performance data. Application Insights: monitors web apps.
Azure DevOps: integrated code deployment and planning. Azure Cognitive Services (AI services): prebuilt AI APIs.
In the portal, use the Advisor blade for security recommendations and the Monitor blade for health of services.

sections.title: Azure Service Health scope
points: Azure Service Health gives a personalized view of the health of the Azure services, regions, and resources you use.
It covers service issues, planned maintenance, and health advisories, and sits alongside Azure status (global) and Resource health (individual resources).
You can create service health alerts to be notified of incidents and planned maintenance.
It reports and notifies; it cannot prevent a service failure.
Azure Advisor gives recommendations; Azure Monitor gives telemetry; neither is the planned maintenance notification service.

sections.title: Finding health notifications in the portal
points: In the portal, Service Health is reached from Help + support and from Azure Monitor.
Use it to view planned maintenance events and service failure notifications that can affect your subscription.
For a VM in a region, check Service Health (under Monitor) for outages in that region and service.

sections.title: Azure Monitor as the central data platform
points: Azure Monitor collects, analyzes, and acts on telemetry from Azure, on-premises, and other clouds, across multiple subscriptions.
Monitor data (metrics and logs) is stored; log data goes to a Log Analytics workspace.
Log Analytics is the tool where you run Kusto (KQL) queries to compare events across many resources.
Azure AD activity logs can be routed to Azure Monitor. Azure Monitor integrates with Application Insights and Log Analytics.
Event Hubs streams events, Stream Analytics processes streams, Service Health is health reporting; they are not the monitoring repository.

sections.title: Azure Monitor alerts
points: Alerts notify you or run automation when a condition is met on metrics, logs (including Log Analytics workspace data), or activity log events.
For example, an activity log alert can fire when an administrator stops a VM.
Alerts use action groups to send notifications such as email, SMS, voice, or push and to trigger webhooks, runbooks, and Logic Apps.
Azure Monitor can monitor on-premises computers, not only Azure VMs.

sections.title: Application Insights
points: Application Insights is an Azure Monitor feature for application performance management.
Use it for web apps: page load times in the browser, request rates, response times, failures, and dependencies.
Log Analytics queries log data, Network Watcher diagnoses networks, and alerts only notify.

sections.title: Activity log: who did what
points: The Azure activity log records subscription-level events: who did what, and when, for write operations such as stopping a VM.
Use it to find which user turned off a VM; it keeps data for a limited time (90 days by default).

sections.title: What an SLA guarantees
points: An Azure SLA is a formal Microsoft commitment to performance standards, mainly uptime (availability), not features, bandwidth, or performance.
Monthly uptime % = (Maximum Available Minutes - Downtime Minutes) / Maximum Available Minutes x 100.
If the SLA is not met, you receive service credits for that service against your bill, not a refund of other services.
Azure SLAs vary by service and configuration; most paid services start at 99.9%. Microsoft Entra ID Premium P2 is covered at 99.9%, whereas Free has no SLA.
Services in preview are excluded from SLAs.

sections.title: Composite SLAs
points: A composite SLA covers an application that depends on multiple services. Multiply the individual SLAs together.
Do not use the minimum, maximum, or divide. Chaining dependencies lowers the composite.
Redundant paths (for example, resources in multiple regions) can raise the effective SLA.

sections.title: Raising availability for a VM workload
points: VM SLAs rise with redundancy: a single VM with premium storage 99.9%, availability sets 99.95%, two or more VMs across availability zones 99.99%.
To reach 99.99%, deploy at least two VMs spread across two or more availability zones; one zone or one VM is not enough.
Deploying to multiple regions can increase guaranteed uptime; buying multiple subscriptions does not.

sections.title: Private preview, public preview, GA
points: Typical lifecycle: private preview, public preview, general availability (GA).
Private preview: invitation only for selected customers. Public preview: available to any customer with an Azure subscription. GA: released to all customers.
Preview services are visible in the regular portal and can be managed with portal, CLI, and PowerShell; the portal labels previews.
Preview pricing is often discounted; GA is billed at normal rates, so the price does not drop at GA.
After GA, services continue to receive new features, and existing preview resources generally need not be recreated.

sections.title: Preview terms: SLA and support
points: Public preview services are excluded from SLAs; each preview defines its own terms and support.
There is no standard SLA percentage for previews.
Previews can technically be used in production but this is not recommended, because there is no SLA guarantee.
Private previews do not require a separate portal.

sections.title: Modern Lifecycle Policy
points: The Modern Lifecycle Policy applies to continuously serviced products and services.
If there is no successor, Microsoft gives at least 12 months' notice before ending support (excluding free services and previews).
There is no fixed five-year mainstream support term under this policy (that is the Fixed Policy).

sections.title: Support plan tiers
points: Basic: included with all subscriptions; 24/7 billing and subscription support, docs, forums, Advisor, and Service Health.
Developer: business-hours technical support by email. Standard: 24/7 technical support by phone and email.
Professional Direct: Standard-level support plus architectural guidance. Premier: highest tier for enterprise customers with an Enterprise Agreement.
An Azure free account has the Basic plan. Community forums are open to everyone, not only pay-as-you-go.
Support requests can be opened under every plan, including Basic (nontechnical for Basic); the plan decides the support type and response.

sections.title: Phone and email access to engineers
points: Basic has no technical support. Developer has email only, during business hours.
Standard, Professional Direct, and Premier include phone and email access to support engineers 24/7.
The lowest-cost plan with 24/7 phone access to engineers is Standard.

sections.title: Architectural guidance
points: Professional Direct includes architecture support and guidance on workload design.
It is the lowest-cost plan offering this; Premier costs more, and Standard/Developer lack it.

sections.title: Opening requests and quota increases
points: Create a support request in the Azure portal, from Help + support, or from a resource's Support + troubleshooting menu.
Quota increases are also requested via Help + support (new support request, quota issue type).
support.microsoft.com is not where Azure support requests are created.

sections.title: Azure Germany
points: Azure Germany was a separate sovereign instance of Azure in German datacenters for data residency.
It was available to eligible customers and partners globally, not only German residents or German-registered enterprises.
The service has been retired in favor of Azure regions in Germany.

sections.title: Azure Blueprints
points: A blueprint packages artifacts into a repeatable definition: ARM templates, Azure Policy assignments, role assignments (RBAC), and resource groups.
You assign a blueprint to a subscription, not to a resource group.
Blueprint resource locks (Read Only or Do Not Delete) are enforced by the assignment and re-applied, even if someone removes the lock manually.
Azure Blueprints (Preview) is scheduled to be retired on January 31, 2027.
